Title: Review: Athens Through the Ages
Description: This volume provides a critical review of Jennifer Tolbert Roberts's book, *Athens on Trial: The Antidemocratic Tradition in Western Thought*, exploring how Athenian democracy has been viewed throughout history and analyzing Roberts's arguments and interpretations.
VolumeSummary: Jennifer Roberts's *Athens on Trial* examines the historical arguments against Athenian democracy, tracing them from ancient Athens to modern scholarship. The book surveys Western opinions on Athenian democracy, both positive and negative, and Roberts clearly supports democratic Athens, believing modern society can learn from it. While Roberts is a skilled historian of ancient institutions, the reviewer, Stephen G. Salkever, notes that she sometimes overlooks complexities, especially in her interpretations of philosophical texts. The book is structured into three main sections: ancient Athenian critics like Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle; views from ancient Rome, Renaissance Italy, and early modern Europe; and finally, 19th and 20th-century scholarly works. Salkever praises the book's extensive documentation and usefulness as a survey, despite finding some of Roberts's philosophical interpretations simplistic.

Pages.Title: Athens Through the Ages Review
Pages.ReferenceSummary: This page reviews Jennifer Tolbert Roberts's book, *Athens on Trial*, which investigates the history of anti-democratic thought concerning ancient Athens. It covers the book's structure, Roberts's main arguments about the historical portrayal of Athenian democracy, and the reviewer's critique of her philosophical interpretations. The review discusses how ancient critics, later European thinkers, and modern scholars have shaped the understanding of Athens, highlighting Roberts's sympathy for democratic Athens.

Content.Text: Jennifer Roberts's book, Athens on Trial: The Antidemocratic Tradition in Western Thought, explores the hostile tradition (negative opinions) about Athenian democracy. Roberts states that these negative views originated in ancient Athens itself. Despite occasionally using rhetorical gestures (persuasive techniques), Roberts's book does not claim to uncover a single, anti-democratic tradition. Instead, Athens on Trial offers a broad and well-researched chronological survey (a historical overview in time order) of Western opinions on Athenian democracy. This survey covers arguments both for and against Athenian democracy, from ancient times to the present. Roberts clearly favors democratic Athens and believes that modern societies can learn from its practices. A repeated idea in her book is that critics of Athens fail to recognize how democratic principles contributed to its creative achievements (significant accomplishments) (p. 312). However, Roberts, as an experienced historian, acknowledges the difficult questions about how much democratic Athens depended on imperialism (expanding power through other territories), chattel slavery, and the lower status of women. She does not always argue that critics of Athenian democracy are simply motivated by class-based opposition to popular rule.
Content.KeyPhrase: Athens on Trial, antidemocratic tradition, chronological survey, creative achievements, Athenian democracy
Content.Question: What is the primary focus of Jennifer Roberts's book, *Athens on Trial*, and what is her general stance on Athenian democracy?

Content.Text: Roberts's book is organized into three parts. The first part examines Athenian critics (people from Athens who criticized the system), particularly Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle, who wrote about Athenian democracy. Roberts believes that the historical reputation of Athenian democracy suffered because it lacked a strong and skilled defender at the time. She sees this absence of native theorizing (developing theories and ideas) as a serious issue because the surviving passages praising democracy show that its supporters had very different ideas about the system's core principles compared to its critics (p. 35). To fill this gap, Roberts gathers texts from Herodotus, the tragedians and orators, Thucydides' Pericles, and Plato's Protagoras. She uses these texts to paint a picture of a vigorous regime (a strong and energetic government) that celebrated human involvement in politics and the arts. This portrayal shows Athenian democracy not just as a defense against tyranny, but as a dynamic entity driven by the combined effort and abilities of all its male citizens (p. 47). While finding strong ancient supporters of this "vital, throbbing entity" (p. 84) is difficult, there were many Greek enemies of Athenian democracy. These critics often shared a class-based critique (criticism based on social and economic class). They saw demo-kratia (rule by the people) as the tyrannical rule of the poor over the rich, believing that rich people made better political decisions (p. 49).
Content.KeyPhrase: Athenian critics, Thucydides, Plato, Aristotle, theorizing, vigorous regime, class-based critique, demo-kratia
Content.Question: How does Roberts attempt to address the perceived lack of a strong defense for Athenian democracy from ancient Athens itself?

Content.Text: The second part of Roberts's book looks at how democratic Athens was viewed by politicians, philosophers, and historians in ancient Rome (the Roman Empire), the city-states of Renaissance Italy (independent cities in Italy during the Renaissance), and Western Europe and North America during the 17th and 18th centuries. These periods involved debates surrounding the revolutions (major political changes) of those centuries. In separate chapters, Roberts explores what was said about Athenian democracy during each period. She also provides explanations for the different views expressed. Roberts emphasizes the wide variety of opinions, and her explanations are generally reasonable and fit the historical context. Unlike the first section, this part of the book does not suggest that critics of Athenian democracy are always class enemies of the people. The reviewer notes that Roberts faces challenges in accurately attributing anti-democratic views to figures like Thucydides, Plato, and Aristotle. She tries to maintain her argument against resistant texts by attributing carelessness (lack of attention) or inconsistency (not staying the same) to these authors. For example, she suggests Thucydides did not think deeply about constitutional questions, and she downplays Plato's critiques of oligarchy, framing him as a typical Greek aristocrat. She also explains Aristotle's praise for collective deliberation as an inconsistency in his generally aristocratic tradition, rather than acknowledging a nuanced position (p. 90).
Content.KeyPhrase: ancient Rome, Renaissance Italy, Western Europe, revolutions, carelessness, inconsistency, Thucydides, Plato, Aristotle
Content.Question: How does Roberts categorize and analyze the historical perspectives on Athenian democracy in the second section of her book?

Content.Text: The final third of the book focuses on more professional and scholarly works (academic writings) from the 19th and 20th centuries. Roberts provides an excellent overview of this period. She describes the eventual triumph (victory) of those who supported Athenian democracy over its critics. Roberts identifies two main reasons for this victory. First, the German Romantics (a cultural movement in Germany) like Herder, Schiller, and Hölderlin sought to find a unified way of life, or a "country of the mind," as a remedy (solution) to the fragmentation caused by modernity. Second, George Grote, a utilitarian scholar and friend of the Mills, significantly contributed to this shift. Grote's History of Greece established democratic Athens as the true origin for the secular liberal democracy (a government system based on individual rights and freedoms, separate from religion) he hoped to see in England. Roberts uses these historical uses of the Greek past as starting points. She then discusses 20th-century writings on Athenian democracy in detail, emphasizing the complex interaction between scholarship (academic study) and political vision (ideas about how society should be governed).
Content.KeyPhrase: scholarly works, triumph, German Romantics, George Grote, secular liberal democracy, scholarship, political vision
Content.Question: According to Roberts, what were the two main factors that led to the eventual widespread acceptance of Athenian democracy in modern scholarship?

Content.Text: The reviewer, Stephen G. Salkever, points out that Roberts is not the most skilled reader of philosophical texts (writings on fundamental questions of existence and knowledge) among current ancient historians. Her comments on discussions of Athens by Machiavelli, Rousseau, and Hegel are similarly weak. Salkever argues that Roberts extracts only clear pro- or anti-Athenian democracy sentiments from their works, ignoring the broader philosophical goals and questions of these writers. For example, she describes Machiavelli as "a man of powerful passions" whose emotions were "intensely engaged by the political turmoil," leading him to have "mixed emotions in Machiavelli" (p. 124). For Hegel, she suggests he "cannot seem to make up his mind" about the figures of Antigone or Creon (p. 218). This philosophical naïveté (lack of experience or wisdom in philosophy) means Roberts treats philosophers as either one-sided political supporters or narrow academics. Salkever believes this approach not only misrepresents philosophy but also removes the deeper philosophical content from politics and scholarship. Despite these shortcomings in interpreting philosophical treatises, Athens on Trial provides valuable material for distinguishing which critical questions about Athens and democracy are still relevant today. The book's weaknesses as an interpretive treatise (a formal written work explaining a subject) do not lessen its significant value as a compendium (a collection of information) that will interest anyone studying modern uses of ancient Greek politics and philosophy.
Content.KeyPhrase: philosophical texts, Machiavelli, Rousseau, Hegel, philosophical naïveté, interpretive treatise, compendium
